blocks.content: Why Databases Exist established that a database makes three promises a plain file cannot: data is never lost, never wrong, and always found quickly. But once you accept that you need a database, a second question follows immediately: which kind. Not every database stores data the same way, and the shape of your data should genuinely drive that choice.

This topic walks through the major database types you will actually encounter in real systems, what each one is genuinely good at, and a worked example showing how a single real application often ends up using more than one type at once, not out of indecision, but because different parts of the system genuinely have different needs.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032140922-772425553.png
blocks.alt: Types of databases follows why databases exist, since different data shapes genuinely need different storage engines

blocks.content: 1. The Real Question Behind Every Database Choice
blocks.text: 1. The Real Question Behind Every Database Choice

blocks.content: Before comparing specific products, it helps to ask three honest questions about your own data. What shape does your data actually have, is it naturally tabular with fixed fields, or does it vary wildly from one record to the next. How will you actually query it later, by a single key, by complex joins across relationships, or by searching flexible attributes.

And how much consistency do you actually need, can a read occasionally return slightly stale data, or must every read reflect the absolute latest write immediately. These three questions, more than any product name, are what actually determine the right database type.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032142922-492631291.png
blocks.alt: The real question behind every database choice: what shape your data has, how you will query it, and how much consistency you actually need

blocks.content: 2. Relational Databases

A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed set of columns, where every row in a table has the same structure. Rows relate to other rows through keys, a customer table connects to an orders table through a shared customer id, and the database itself enforces those relationships.

This model is genuinely strong when your data has clear structure and clear relationships that matter, orders belong to customers, customers have addresses, addresses belong to specific orders. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle are the products most engineers encounter in this category.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032144452-849514530.png
blocks.alt: Relational databases store data in fixed column tables, with rows related to other rows through keys, examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle

3. Document Databases

A document database stores data as flexible, JSON like documents, where different documents in the same collection can genuinely have different fields. There is no fixed schema enforced across every document the way a relational table enforces fixed columns.

This model genuinely fits data that naturally varies, a product catalog where different product categories have wildly different attributes, a shoe has a size, a laptop has a processor, and forcing both into identical fixed columns would waste a lot of empty space. MongoDB and Couchbase are common examples.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032146035-823513324.png
blocks.alt: Document databases store flexible, JSON like documents with no fixed schema required across documents, examples include MongoDB and Couchbase

blocks.content: 4. Key Value Stores

A key value store is the simplest model of all, data is just a key mapped directly to a value, with no relationships, no fixed schema, nothing beyond that direct mapping. Looking something up means asking for a specific key and getting its value back immediately.

This simplicity is exactly what makes key value stores extremely fast for lookups by a known key, a user session, a cache entry, a rate limit counter. Redis and DynamoDB are the products most engineers reach for in this category.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032147620-71989429.png
blocks.alt: Key value stores map a key directly to a value with extremely fast lookups, examples include Redis and DynamoDB

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Assuming a key value store can replace a relational database entirely because it feels simpler to use. Key value stores are genuinely fast for direct lookups, but they cannot enforce relationships between records the way a relational database does.
5. Other Specialized Models

A few more specialized database types show up for specific needs. Columnar databases store data by column rather than by row, which makes aggregating a single column across huge numbers of rows genuinely fast, Cassandra is a common example. Graph databases treat relationships themselves as the actual data being stored and queried, genuinely useful when the connections between things matter more than the things themselves, Neo4j is a common example.

And time series databases are optimized specifically for timestamped data arriving in order, sensor readings, metrics, logs, InfluxDB is a common example. Each of these exists because a general purpose relational or document database handles that specific pattern less efficiently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032149180-281902019.png
blocks.alt: Other specialized models: columnar for fast column aggregation, graph for relationship heavy data, and time series for timestamped data

blocks.content: 6. A Worked Example

A concrete scenario shows these types working together in one real system. Building an e commerce order system genuinely benefits from using more than one database type at once, matched to what each part of the system actually needs.

Orders and payments genuinely need a relational database, since strict consistency matters, an order total must always match its line items exactly. The product catalog fits a document store well, since different product categories have flexible, varying attributes. And the session cart fits a key value store well, since it needs extremely fast reads and writes tied to a single session key.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032150744-714907995.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: an e commerce system using relational for orders and payments, document store for the catalog, and key value for the session cart

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A single real application often genuinely uses more than one database type at once, not out of indecision, but because different parts of the system have genuinely different data shapes and consistency needs.
7. Choosing Wisely

Defaulting to one familiar database type for every part of a system, purely out of habit or comfort, creates real friction wherever the data shape does not actually fit that model well, forcing flexible data into rigid tables, or forcing relationship heavy data into a model with no real join support.

Matching database type to the actual shape of the data lets each part of the system use the right tool, at the cost of slightly more operational complexity, running and understanding more than one kind of database at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032152235-82581987.png
blocks.alt: Defaulting to one database type for everything creates friction where the data does not fit; matching type to actual data shape gives each part of the system the right tool

9. A Quick Reference Query
Here is a simple relational query, the kind that becomes natural once you are working with a relational database specifically, selecting a customer name alongside their most recent order date.

SELECT customers.name, MAX(orders.order_date) AS last_order
FROM customers
JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
GROUP BY customers.name;

FROM customers

GROUP BY customers.name;

blocks.content: 10. Common Mistakes

["Choosing a database type based on popularity rather than data shape: a trendy choice that does not fit your actual data creates real, ongoing friction.","Assuming one database type must handle an entire system: different parts of a real system often genuinely have different needs.","Ignoring consistency requirements when picking a type: a system that needs strict consistency should not default to a model built for flexibility over consistency."]
items: Choosing a database type based on popularity rather than data shape: a trendy choice that does not fit your actual data creates real, ongoing friction.
Assuming one database type must handle an entire system: different parts of a real system often genuinely have different needs.
Ignoring consistency requirements when picking a type: a system that needs strict consistency should not default to a model built for flexibility over consistency.

Relational databases fit structured data with clear, enforced relationships, examples include PostgreSQL and MySQL.
Document databases fit flexible, varying data with no fixed schema, examples include MongoDB and Couchbase.
Key value stores fit extremely fast lookups by a known key, examples include Redis and DynamoDB.
